title: Body condition scoring pigs
subtitle: A hands-on check to keep your pigs neither thin nor fat.
excerpt: Body condition scoring (BCS) is the practical method for deciding whether a pig is carrying too much or too little fat. Scales run from 1 (emaciated) to 5 (obese), with 3 the target for most smallholding pigs. The assessment takes 30 seconds per animal and needs no equipment.
sourceNotes: AHDB Pork Body Condition Scoring in Sows factsheet (2019). DEFRA Code of Practice for the Welfare of Pigs (2003), nutrition and condition section. Quality Meat Scotland, Pig Management Handbook (2020).

glossaryTerms.definition: A 1 to 5 scale measuring the fat cover on a pig by feel. Score 3 is the working target for most sows and growers.
The prominent bone at the rear flank of a pig. The easiest single reference point for BCS assessment.

content.text: Body condition scoring a pig tells you whether her feed ration needs adjusting. You do it by pressing your fingers over the bones at the back and loin, and scoring what you feel. An overweight sow has difficulty farrowing and often has poor litters. An underweight sow loses condition rapidly during lactation. Score every sow monthly and at weaning.
What the scores mean
Score 1 (emaciated): the spine, ribs, and hip bones are visible and angular. The pig needs immediate attention.
Score 2 (thin): bones easy to feel with no pressure; ribs visible on a lean pig. Feed rate needs increasing.
Score 3 (ideal): bones can be felt with firm pressure; no sharp edges; a slight covering of fat. This is the target for sows at mating and farrowing.
Score 4 (fat): bones need hard pressure to find; the pig's outline is smooth and rounded. Feed rate needs reducing.
Score 5 (obese): bones cannot be felt at all. The pig will struggle to rise and may have joint problems. Restrict feed significantly.
How to score a pig
Approach the pig calmly and let her come to you if she is halter-trained or used to handling. Press firmly with your fingertips at these three reference points.
The spine in the loin region, between the last rib and the pelvis. Press the heel of your hand along the centre line. A score 3 spine has a slight groove but no sharp ridge.
The ribs, from the mid-section downward. Count from the rump forward; a score 3 pig has ribs you can feel clearly but only with firm pressing.
The
hip bone
at the rear flank. The pin bones project just to either side of the tail. On a score 3 pig they are covered but findable. On a score 2 pig they stick out.

Use all three points together to assign a single score. If they disagree (the loin says 3 but the ribs say 2), score conservatively. A half-score (2.5, 3.5) is acceptable when the pig sits between two categories.
Target
BCS
at different stages
At mating: score 3. A thin sow has reduced ovulation rate. A fat sow has impaired heat detection.
At farrowing: score 3.0 to 3.5. A sow farrowing at score 4 or above is at higher risk of difficulty.
At weaning: score 2.5 to 3. Lactation draws on body reserves; losing one score unit during a 4-week lactation is normal. Losing more than that means she was underfed.
Growers and finishers: assess every 2 weeks and adjust feed accordingly. Pigs reaching the abattoir at over BCS 4 carry excess backfat and will grade poorly.
Recording and acting on the score

Record the date, the individual pig ID (ear tag), and the score in your holding health diary. A trend over three assessments tells you more than a single score. If a sow consistently scores below 2.5, investigate: consider worm burden, tooth problems, or competition at the trough if she is group-housed.

attrs.cue: Pig is BCS 2 but eating well
attrs.cause: High worm burden reducing nutrient absorption, or trough competition in a group
attrs.fix: Worm at the rate on the label. If group-housed, check that she is getting to the trough. Add a second feeding point if necessary.

attrs.cue: Sow stays at BCS 3.5 or 4 despite reducing feed
attrs.cause: Too much forage or ad-lib access to root crops, or she is building condition ahead of farrowing
attrs.fix: Check all feed sources including any rooting areas. Aim to arrive at farrowing at BCS 3, not higher; adjust from two months before farrowing onwards.
